name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: All you need to know about Louisiana’s property tax constitutional amendments
text:
Five of the 10 constitutional amendments on Louisiana's Nov. 3 election ballot would change property tax laws. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana voters will consider 10 constitutional amendments on the Nov. 3 ballot, half of which would change the amount of property tax collected that fund police, parks and public schools.
If approved, the proposals could provide enhanced tax breaks for certain military veterans’ families, senior citizens, people with disabilities and those who fix up blighted properties. One would also give new flexibility to local taxing authorities. 

Elected officials have limited options when they want to make property tax policy changes because all such laws are embedded into the Louisiana Constitution and require a statewide vote to change them. For example, if legislators or the governor want to create a new property tax exemption or enhance an existing one, even for only one parish, they typically have to get a constitutional amendment approved.

Jan Moller who leads Invest in Louisiana, a progressive think tank, said the constitution’s grip on property tax laws means voters are frequently asked to make decisions that impact very few citizens.

For example, Amendment 1 allows surviving spouses of deceased disabled veterans to transfer a property tax exemption to a new house. It is expected to affect a small group of people, as only 229 people claimed the exemption last year, according to a legislative fiscal analysis.  

“This isn’t going to break the bank for any local government because it only applies to maybe a dozen people at most,” Moller said last week at an online forum the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana hosted.
There are arguments for making it difficult to change property tax policy, said Steven Procopio, PAR’s president, in an interview this week. If property taxes laws weren’t in the constitution and didn’t require a statewide vote, legislators might be tempted to lower them to unsustainable levels, he said. 

Property tax cuts are popular, but state lawmakers don’t have to deal with the consequences because they affect local government and school system revenue, Procopio added.

The number of property tax amendments on this year’s ballot could be the result of bottled-up demand, said Sen. Franklin Foil, R-Baton Rouge, chairman of the Senate Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Committee that vetted all the proposals.

There has been a push over the past few years to expand Louisiana’s popular homestead exemption, which waives homeowners from paying taxes on the first $75,000 value of their primary residence. As those efforts stalled, legislators came back with proposals offering more narrow tax relief, said Foil, who sponsored Amendment 1.  
Opposition to the property tax amendments has created strange political bedfellows. Conservative and liberal policy groups have come out against many of the proposals, though for different reasons. 

The Power Coalition for Equality and Justice, an organization that promotes progressive policies on matters such as criminal justice and voting rights, is against all five property tax amendments. 

“Expanding property tax breaks means less money for schools and local services,” the group stated on its website about a few of the amendments. 

Meanwhile, the Pelican Institute for Public Policy, a conservative group that generally pushes for tax reductions, is opposed to four of the property tax amendments. The organization has come out against amendments 1, 6, 9 and 10 because they single out special groups of people — like spouses of deceased veterans, senior citizens and blighted property developers — for tax breaks. It creates an unequal system overall, where people are paying different tax rates for similar properties, said Daniel Erspamer, the institute’s chief executive officer. 

“If you have a certain amount of money to raise to meet a budget, and you give one group or several sets of groups special treatment, you lower rates or lower assessment for one group of people … You have to raise it on someone else,” Erspamer said during the PAR forum last week.
The following summaries cover the property tax-related proposals on the statewide Nov. 3 ballot: 
Amendment 1
The surviving spouse of a military veteran who had a disability related to their service could continue claiming a property tax exemption even if they move out of the home they purchased with their late partner.


Enabling legislation: Act 39 
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027
Supporters: Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs, Leaders for a Better Louisiana
Opponents: Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 2
Local governments could remove existing deadlines, tied to property reassessment cycles, to raise property tax rates to the maximum amount allowed. It’s aimed at allowing local governments to keep property tax rates lower for a longer period of time. Under the current system, local officials have said they feel pressure to sometimes raise rates prematurely because if they don’t, they lose the ability to do so in the future. Opponents argue the proposal would create more uncertainty for taxpayers about when their property tax bills would be raised and by how much. 

Voters rejected a similar amendment in November 2022. Supporters say the ballot language is clearer now and expect a better outcome.


Enabling legislation: Act 273 
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, Pelican Institute, Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Louisiana Chemical Association, Police Jury Association of Louisiana, Louisiana Municipal Association 
Opponents: Power Coalition

Amendment 6
Local governments could increase the homestead exemption for many people 65 and older if their parish or municipality’s voters approved a tax break for seniors through a separate, local ballot initiative. Only households with income of $100,000 or less — or a higher threshold when that income cap is adjusted for inflation — would qualify. The surviving spouse of a deceased person who received this more generous tax break could also claim it as long as they are only five years younger than their partner who died.
This proposal has the ability to affect tens of thousands of Louisiana households, as 184,000 people claimed the underlying exemption for seniors in 2025, according to a legislative fiscal analysis. 

Enabling legislation: Act 274
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2028 
Supporters: No prominent organizations have come forward to endorse this amendment. 
Opponents: Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 9
Under current law, people 65 or older, disabled veterans, other residents who are totally and permanently disabled, and the spouses of military members killed or missing in action qualify for a special property tax freeze. This proposal would raise the existing income threshold for people to qualify for those enhanced tax breaks from $100,000 to $150,000 per household. The threshold would be adjusted to match inflation rates in future years. Around 422,000 properties were subject to the existing special exemption in 2024, according to a legislative fiscal analysis. 

Enabling legislation: Act 220 of 2025

Enabling legislation: Act 220 of 2025
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: No prominent organizations have come forward to endorse this amendment. 
Opponents: Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 10
Local governments could adopt property tax breaks for blighted properties once they are rehabilitated. For derelict residential property, up to 75% of its renovated assessed value could qualify for exemption for 20 years. For vacant, unimproved land next to a residence or commercial building, up to 25% of its assessed value could qualify for 10 years. 


Enabling legislation: Act 272
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, Leaders for a Better Louisiana 
Opponents: Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Senate President Ben Albritton says he’ll vote ‘no’ on property tax cuts
text:
Senate President Ben Albritton talks to reporters following the 2026 session Sine Die on March 13, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Less than five months after Florida Senate President Ben Albritton hailed his chamber for voting to put a measure on the Nov. 3 ballot seeking a major expansion of the homestead property tax exemption for non-school taxes, he now says he opposes the proposal.
“As a native of Florida’s heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart. It’s who I am,” Albritton says in a statement posted on the Florida Sherriff’s Association social media page. “Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida’s rural counties, gutting essential services for law enforcement, emergency response services, and critical infrastructure.”
Albritton goes to say the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission is scheduled to meet in 2027 and suggests that is a better venue to vet such a major proposal. Both the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Florida TaxWatch have made similar remarks.
If approved by 60% of the voters on Nov. 3, Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for all non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It creates a process for the Florida Legislature to allow counties and cities to expand the exemption further, potentially eliminating all non-school homestead property taxes over time.
Opponents have warned that loss of tax revenue could put damaging pressure on local budgets, public safety, and other community services. State economists have estimated that, if passed, Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.
That’s why it’s opposed by organizations throughout the state, including the Florida Sheriffs Association, the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, and the Florida Association of Professional Firefighters.
Albritton has previously said he “stands with law enforcement” regarding issues such as firearms regulations, and he repeated that in his statement, saying, “I proudly stand with the Florida Sheriffs, first responders and my neighbors across rural Florida.”
Albritton’s announcement is a bit of an about-face. After the Florida Senate this June voted to put the property tax cut plan on the ballot, Albritton hailed the decision.
“Owning your own home has been the American dream since our nation was founded 250 years ago. What better way to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary than a massive property tax cut through a $250,000 homestead exemption for Floridians,” Albritton said on June 2 in a written statement.
“I’m grateful to Governor DeSantis for leading the conversation on cutting property taxes and putting forward this robust proposal for the consideration of Florida voters this fall. For our part, the Senate has consistently advocated for an amendment that is significant and straightforward — a $250,000 homestead exemption in honor of America’s 250th birthday achieves that goal and then some.”
Albritton represents all of Charlotte, DeSoto, and Hardee counties and parts of Lee and Polk counties in the Florida Senate. Although his tenure as president of the Senate ends next month, he won’t be term-limited out of his seat until 2028.
Florida’s previous Senate President, Kathleen Passidomo, also recently announced that she, too, will vote against Amendment 3.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont taxpayers can’t compare school budgets. The state could fix that.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Rkiouak, founder of Hunger Mountain Intelligence, a growth and automation consultancy for small and mid-sized businesses.
Every March, Vermonters vote on school budgets they cannot compare with the district next door. Each district lays out its budget differently. What one district calls “special education shared services” is three separate lines in the next. When a budget goes up, the explanation is a list of pressures: health insurance, special education, enrollment. Voters have no way to tell whether those pressures are bigger here than next door.
The state’s reports should settle this. Instead, they contradict each other. The Agency of Education’s staff survey is the only place every district’s positions and pay are coded the same way. Yet for one district, it lists 7.2 teaching positions costing $4.9 million. For the same district, it shows $18 million in salaries and no benefits, while federal census figures show $6.9 million in benefits. 
To compare districts, the state divides each one’s spending by a weighted pupil count, known as LTWADM. The count starts with resident students and adds extra weight for those who cost more to educate, including students from low-income families, older students, English learners, and students in small schools or sparsely populated areas. The state published the breakdown of that count for 2025-26 in January 2025. It hasn’t done so for 2026-27.
I wanted to see how my own district, Washington Central, compares with four nearby districts. Washington Central runs six schools. Measured per weighted pupil, and leaving out debt payments and building projects, it spends about $2.3 million a year more than it would at the average rate of Harwood, Montpelier Roxbury, Mount Abraham and Barre. 
Most of the gap is pay. Washington Central’s average teacher salary on the staff survey, $79,827, is the highest of the five. Higher pay rates, not more teachers, explain most of the difference. Its superintendent is the lowest paid of the five. But its special education director and curriculum director are the highest paid in their roles, and its administrative costs are second only to Mount Abraham’s. 
Building costs rose by a third over three years while consumer prices rose about 13%. Special education and student support spending grew 36%, nearly half the district’s total increase. Yet its cost per child with an individualized education program is at the neighbors’ average.
The district’s annual report includes an enrollment table where the school columns don’t add up to the totals in any of the seven years. This year’s budget comes in two versions, one for three elementary schools and one for five. They have the same total but different line items, and nothing shows how money moved between them. 
The district estimated that closing two schools would save $881,920 in 2024 and $1,088,508 in 2025. In January 2026, it said neither figure “is accurate data as of our current budget scenario.” It has not published the model behind them. Calais and Worcester voters rejected the closure of their elementary schools in February, but in August district voters gave all five towns a say in future closures. My own math, using the district’s salary roster and enrollment projections, puts the savings at $1.5 million to $1.9 million a year. I may be wrong, but there’s no published figure to check it against.
None of this is unique to Washington Central. It is what the rules allow. 
Vermont requires districts to file budgets on the state’s form and report staff to its survey. It then compares them using a pupil count it hasn’t fully published this year. Under Act 73, passed in 2025, the state would pay each district a set amount per weighted pupil, starting in 2029 if certain conditions are met. A formula that pays per pupil makes one question central: What does it cost to run a school here, compared with there? Right now, the state cannot answer it.
Three things would fix that. The Legislature and the Agency of Education can make all three.
First, require every district to publish its general ledger by purpose and type of expense, in a spreadsheet, on the state’s chart of accounts, with its position roster by year. Not a budget book. The ledger.
Second, have the state publish its own calculations every year, once they’re final: the weighted pupil count broken down for every district, as it did for 2025-26; special education cost reports for every year; and the per-pupil spending measured the same way from year to year. 
Third, reconcile the three sets of numbers that describe each district: the district’s budget, the state’s surveys, and federal census and education reports. Where they disagree, say which is right and why. That takes staff and money, and the Legislature should fund it.
Vermont’s new education law puts pressure on small schools, and state spending limits tighten every year from 2028. Voters will be asked to approve whatever comes next. They should be able to see, in numbers that mean the same thing in every town, what their district spends and what the alternatives would cost.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont taxpayers can’t compare school budgets. The state could fix that..

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: 18 changes suggested for state funding, local property taxes for K-12 schools
text:
Former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, center, speaks at a meeting of Nebraska's School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. At left is Tom Briese, a former state treasurer and former state senator from Albion. At right is Grant Latimer, a policy adviser to Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Among recommendations to increase state funding for Nebraska’s 244 school districts was one adopted Tuesday to increase per-student aid by at least 4% annually.
A draft of the 16-page report from Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission offers 18 recommendations, most of which would tweak the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act, known as TEEOSA. The formula distributes state aid to school districts statewide. This includes the annual bump of at least 4% in foundation aid per student, from $1,500 to $1,560 for the 2027-28 school year.
Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission meets on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In addition to the recommendations, a portion of Tuesday’s discussion featured a guideline to policymakers that state support for K-12 schools be maintained at 51% alongside local property taxes.
“I applaud the work of the commission and what’s being presented here, but we have to be much more ambitious in what we propose here somewhere,” said Commissioner Tom Briese, Nebraska’s former state treasurer (2023-25) and a former state senator from Albion (2017-23).
The recommendations head to the 49-member Legislature. Lawmakers will have final say on whether to adopt any of the suggestions.
‘Not in the cards’
Briese and others suggested that the 51% state contribution was the bare minimum. In Briese’s view, that number should be “substantially higher,” as high as the state taking on 100% of K-12 operational expenses to offset the largest source of local property taxes.
“That’s not in the cards at this date, but I’m pretty confident there’s several folks in here that’d like to see something far above 51%,” Briese said.
Associate Superintendent Liz Standish of Lincoln Public Schools speaks at a meeting of Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil, chair of the Legislature’s Education Committee, said he, too, was thankful for but not satisfied with the recommendations. He is one of three non-voting lawmakers serving on the commission.
Associate Superintendent Liz Standish of Lincoln Public Schools said the commission had not discussed the state-local mix in a year. She said she felt uncomfortable stating in the report that the number should be increased until the commission deliberated further.
What’s the right state-local mix?
Standish said “huge progress has been made” with state funding support, which districts appreciate. But she encouraged commissioners to utilize new data that Nebraska Department of Education staff helped compile and consider the state-local percentage next year.
“All I’m asking for is let’s reflect on where we are with this new data set that we’ve studied over the course of the last year and then, as a commission, have time for deliberative conversation about, OK, what do we think the right mix in Nebraska might be?” Standish said.
The new Nebraska School Financing Review Commission receives a briefing on the various components that make up the state’s mainline school funding formula under the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunity Support Act, better known as TEEOSA. Sept. 22, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, who chaired the Legislature’s Revenue Committee for six years, said it was OK for the commission to say commissioners disagreed.
“I think to turn in a report of this diverse of a group and say we all agree on everything … if I were a senator, I would find that doubtful,” Linehan said. “I’d be calling each of you and saying, ‘Did you agree with this?’”
Reaching consensus
Superintendent John Schwartz of Millard Public Schools, the commission vice chair, suggested that instead of saying “no consensus,” the commission could phrase it more positively. He suggested adding that “additional processing is needed to see if a consensus on what the state funding level target should be.”
Linehan said it was pretty clear the commission is divided and that the lack of consensus isn’t a secret, “nor should it be a secret.” She said money appropriated to public schools should keep going to public schools.
Superintendent John Schwartz of Millard Public Schools, vice chair of the School Financing Review Commission. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The commission ultimately amended the report to state: “While the commission agrees that the state’s contribution should be maintained at a minimum of 51%, there is currently no consensus regarding the appropriate level of state funding beyond that threshold.”
One notable school district, Omaha Public Schools, has opposed increased reliance on state funding, a point of contention in Nebraska’s 2024 special session focused on property taxes. 
Shavonna Holman, who sits on the OPS board and the commission, was not present Tuesday.
Increased aid to school districts
Lawmakers, with Gov. Jim Pillen’s backing, created the commission in 2025 to improve Nebraska state funding for K-12 schools with the goal of also mitigating property tax increases.
Eight of the commission’s proposed adjustments would amend caps for local spending, such as providing three-year averages for enrollment calculations and changing factors for limited English proficiency and poverty considerations.
Other recommendations would tweak factors in TEEOSA, such as calculating poverty, limited English proficiency, technological needs and basic year-over-year funding.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, addresses the new School Financing Review Commission during its first meeting. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
If adopted, schools would be allowed to carry forward unused property tax authority under their base cap, such as if they increased spending by less than 3% when the base cap was 3%. But the recommendations call for wiping out built-up taxing authority over the past three years if it came from an override vote and was not used in that same year.
“Collectively, these changes reflect measured changes to the existing revenue cap which better align with the intent of the legislation while preserving local control. These changes also make adjustments to reflect the impact data on the operation of the cap since its inception,” the report states.
If all of the recommendations had been adopted before the 2026-27 school year, the commission estimated nearly $55.5 million more aid to local school districts.
In total, 232 school districts would have seen an increase in aid, up to 43.32%, while 12 would have received a slight decrease, between 0.42% and 14.11%.
TEEOSA would have risen to $1.15 billion in state aid being distributed to school districts.
For 2026-27, TEEOSA consists of calculating a school district’s “resources” — six different sources, including an estimated property tax calculation based on district valuations — minus a district’s “needs” — 18 categories, including poverty, transportation, summer school, limited English proficiency and student growth. 
All school districts receive foundation aid, but districts only receive additional “equalization aid” if their needs are greater than their resources. Only 44 of 244 districts were equalized this year.
Property taxes and the state budget
As of current state budget projections, lawmakers will need to close a $209 million deficit through mid-2027 by May of next year. At the same time, lawmakers must address that hole and the $847 million that would grow if left unchecked by mid-2029.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward speaks at a meeting of Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. At left is state Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln. Both are non-voting members of the commission. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln, who will introduce the revenue side of changes that the commission has recommended, said the commission has been focused on determining what would serve schools but also Nebraska taxpayers.
“While we do have an upcoming session that will have budgetary challenges, I think it’s important that we do everything we can not to compromise on what would be the best possible policy that we can create,” Bostar said.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, whose 2025 legislation created the commission, said she plans to introduce the suggested TEEOSA changes if she’s reelected in two weeks. She said cleaning up part of the formula will be a “slam dunk.” The other, more challenging part is the increased foundation aid. 
Hughes said the commission and lawmakers alike don’t want the 51% state support to backslide, and lawmakers will see if they can reach the suggested 4% minimum increase. She said it needs to be a priority in 2027.
“It’s going to be some hard conversations of where do we want to spend,” Hughes said. “All I keep hearing about, in addition to affordability, is the property tax issue.”
How big of a budget hole the Legislature will need to fill will be finalized at an economic forecasting meeting next week. Linehan and Briese are new members of that board, too.
‘Work is just beginning’
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher, who chairs the commission, said he was thankful the commission has twice unanimously approved an annual report, which he joked will prevent some sleepless nights, at least for him.
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher. Aug. 8, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“It’s also not reflective that our work is done,” Maher said of the 2026 report. “I think, as it’s been stated many times today, in some ways, our work is just beginning.”
The commission’s approval authorized an internal executive committee to polish up the report, up to non-substantive changes, and submit it to the Legislature by the Nov. 1 deadline.
The commission will next meet in the first quarter of 2027. The legislative session begins Jan. 6.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Pain from the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ is coming after the midterms. Missouri isn’t ready.
text:
(Getty Images).The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the legislation President Donald Trump called the “One Big Beautiful Bill” would increase the federal deficit by $3.4 trillion over a decade, despite its massive cuts to healthcare and food assistance. It was designed so that its worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the midterm elections. 
Now the midterms are nigh, and Missouri has done too little to mitigate the coming pain.
Cuts to Medicaid are not popular. That’s why congressional Republicans denied they were cutting Medicaid in the legislation. And yet, Republicans looking for offsets to renew tax cuts passed in the first Trump administration found what the CBO estimates will be a $911 billion reduction in federal Medicaid spending over a decade. The law is expected to leave 10 million more Americans uninsured.
Health policy organization KFF estimates $326 billion of the Medicaid spending reductions will come from the legislation’s imposition of “work requirements” on people who are eligible for Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act expansion. Numerous studies show that people on Medicaid who can work are already working. Work requirements do not increase employment, just paperwork.
The savings will come from working poor people and people too disabled to work losing their health insurance, despite remaining eligible, because of administrative burdens that they can’t handle — or their states can’t handle. 
Missouri is terrible at administering benefits generally and particularly unprepared for this.
From January 2025 through February 2026, 333,265 Missourians lost Medicaid coverage, 91.9% of them not because the Missouri Department of Social Services found them ineligible, but for paperwork reasons. 
People lose coverage when they don’t receive their renewal letters, when the letters are confusing, when their work hours vary, when they can’t get ahold of the department after hours on hold, when the agency loses their documents or when the agency receives their documents but doesn’t process them before the computer automatically terminates their coverage. 
That’s without the federal work requirements that take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It’s also without the new federal requirement that Medicaid expansion enrollees renew every 6 months.  Imposing that hurdle is expected to “save” another $63 billion when eligible people lose their insurance.
Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy is tracking states’ readiness to implement the law’s Medicaid requirements across eight metrics: call center wait times, call abandonment rates, application processing times, renewal rate, ex parte renewals (when the state uses data it already has to determine eligibility), disenrollments at renewal, disenrollments for procedural reasons and pending renewals. Missouri was one of three states to earn a red flag for 7 of the 8 metrics.
Cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or “SNAP,” formerly known as food stamps, will bring additional hardship. The law delays one major change until after the midterms: Beginning in October 2027, states with sufficiently high payment error rates will have to pay a portion of SNAP benefit costs for the first time. How much they pay will depend on their error rates, which measure overpayments and underpayments, often resulting from minor mistakes. 
Missouri has a history of failing to administer SNAP in compliance with the law. A federal lawsuit documented disabled people waiting on hold with the department’s call center for many hours only to have their calls dropped and their applications terminated. 
On Oct. 1, Missouri began requiring applicants and people renewing their SNAP benefits to provide additional documentation of their eligibility, in an apparent attempt to lower the error rate that will determine how much Missouri must pay for SNAP. 
Missouri’s error rate dropped from 9.42% in 2024 to 8.26% in 2025. But in the eight months after Missouri’s more stringent documentation requirements went into effect, 46,630 fewer Missourians received benefits.  
If Missouri’s error rate stays in the same range, the state will need to pay an estimated $150 million previously covered by the federal government.
The “One Big Beautiful Bill” has been a freight train headed toward us for a long time. Our representatives did nothing to stop it and little to prepare for it. U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley did so much talking about his opposition to Medicaid cuts, some of us thought he was serious. Instead he voted for the legislation despite it having $340 billion more cuts on top of the work requirements. Those cuts put an estimated 446 hospitals at risk of closing, nine of them in Missouri. Hawley said he’d work to restore the funding just after he voted to cut it. That entailed introducing a messaging bill that has no chance of going anywhere.
U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt and all of our Republican Congressional representatives voted for it as well.  
With the freight train approaching, our Republican state lawmakers put their all into an attempt to eliminate the income tax that voters rejected in August. A plan for filling our coming $1.7 billion budget hole has not been forthcoming.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis schools state takeover paused again
text:
Control of Memphis-Shelby County Schools returns to the local school board as the state takeover faces another court-ordered pause. (Andrea Morales / For Chalkbeat)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Did you know search engines like Google are changing the way you see news? Keep Chalkbeat’s valuable education coverage at the top of your feeds by clicking here and checking the box next to our name.
The state takeover of Memphis-Shelby County Schools has once again been temporarily blocked, this time by a local judge on Monday.
That decision came minutes before the state-appointed oversight board was set to meet for the second time this month, oversight board Chair Billy Orgel said. The ruling throws control of the district back into uncertainty, returning full authority to the local school board only days after a federal judge reinstated the oversight board’s authority.
The federal case over whether the takeover is constitutional remains ongoing. But MSCS and Shelby County leaders filed a separate lawsuit against the takeover law in chancery court on Oct. 7.
As of Monday afternoon, the court order was not available on the Shelby County Chancery Court website. But in a request for a temporary block filed Sunday, district leaders amended their complaint to remove allegations that the state takeover law violates the Tennessee Constitution, a key argument in their federal case.
Instead, the plaintiffs argue that the takeover was ordered without evidence that the district qualified for it and that the takeover will irreparably harm district operations.
Orgel said Monday’s meeting had been canceled around 12:50 p.m., 10 minutes before it was scheduled to begin virtually.
“Hopefully this will be resolved soon so all of us can get together and improve our school system,” Orgel said in a statement to Chalkbeat.
At its first meeting in months earlier this month, the nine-member oversight board fast-tracked approval of key policies and processes to prove it was ready to begin its work. That included a draft approval process for contracts over $50,000.
The draft plan, along with job descriptions for an executive director and oversight board procedures, came from Florida-based consulting group MGT. The firm, which had also advised the state takeover of Houston schools in 2023, was hired by local philanthropists including longtime state takeover supporter Seeding Success.
Editor’s note: This is an ongoing story and will be updated as it develops. 
Bri Hatch covers Memphis-Shelby County Schools for Chalkbeat Tennessee. Reach Bri at bhatch@chalkbeat.org.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Enrollment-calculation trapdoor will squeeze Iowa’s public schools
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds was joined by Des Moines Prep students, state legislators and other charter school advocates as she signed into law a measure making changes to charter school and homeschooling regulations May 12, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed Senate File 2201, the school funding bill, into law on Feb. 26. The 2% increase in per-pupil funding for the 2026-27 school year works out to $160 more per student. When the decline in public enrollment is taken into account, it’s a statewide increase of $17 million from last year’s allotment.
The law includes a massive change in calculation of enrollment formulas. Instead of a single count of certified enrollment taken Oct. 15, a second count has been added to take place on Jan. 15/the third Monday in January called “adjusted enrollment.” (Because of Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the de facto date can be as late as Jan. 18.) The average of these two numbers will become the “basic enrollment” number used for determining the following school year’s funding.
That means the tally used for calculating state supplemental aid will be an approximation in mid-November and not exact until early February. This will end up in conflict with the law requiring state aid to be set within 30 days of the governor’s budget proposal — a deadline that has repeatedly been blown. But that’s OK, since the Legislature can exempt itself from following the law.



Quotation







“The requirement of section 257.8, subsection 1, regarding the enactment of bills establishing the regular program state percent of growth within thirty days of the submission in the year preceding the base year of the governor’s budget does not apply to this division of this Act.”


– SF 2201, bottom of page 4


This change also runs closer to the deadlines schools are under to submit property tax rates (March 5) and finalize budgets (April 30). A bill that passed the House but stalled in the Senate would have limited schools to using the previous year’s allowable growth rate if state aid is not set by March 5 and enabled updates after the fact.
During debate on SF 2201, Sen. Lynn Evans, R-Aurelia, said the second enrollment count would help in situations where a student moves into a district after Oct. 15. Under the current formulas, that student’s enrollment wouldn’t get counted toward funding until two school years later.
That may sound reasonable, but the overwhelming majority of Iowa districts are losing enrollment, and this only applies to changes in the student body over a three-month period.
The trapdoor with this second count was sprung in a different bill, House File 2754, which mainly concerns charter schools. Rep. Skyler Wheeler, R-Hull, said in opening remarks on the House floor April 16: “This is our One Big Beautiful School Choice Bill, or the one-double-B-S-C-B as we like to call it. This bill is big, and it is beautiful.”
HF 2754 includes a section allowing applications for a student to leave a public school at semester break and take half the value of that year’s state cost per pupil with them as education savings account money. An e-mail from IDOE’s Heather Doe said data updated with the second count “will include certified enrollment counts for public districts and the second ESA student enrollment period.” The exact dollar amount in ESAs overall will depend on it.
On April 27, the same evening that the Senate sent HF 2754 to the governor, the Cedar Rapids Community School District voted to close six schools and reconfigure its entire grade lineup starting in 2027. (Reynolds signed the bill May 12, during National Charter Schools Week, while surrounded by charter school students and advocates.) Another division of HF 2754 puts teacher salary supplement funding in the bundle of money that goes with each student from a public school to a charter school. Based on information from the Legislative Services Agency, that would have cost the Cedar Rapids district an additional $270,000 this past year.
“The continual attacks, generally speaking, against the ESA program I find to be fascinating,” Wheeler said on April 16. “I find it to be fascinating entirely because it has been effective. Parents have been empowered. And so we’re going to get upset, generally speaking, because parents were given the ability to go a different route. There hasn’t been a mass exodus.”
Public school enrollment in Iowa for 2025-26 had the most substantial yearly decreases, in both number and percent, in four decades, while private school enrollment increased 26% in three years to a level not seen in a quarter-century. If that’s not a “mass exodus,” what is?
Who’s not complaining?


Last winter, the Senate wanted a 1.75% increase in state aid, the House wanted 2.25%, and the compromise was 2%. The difference in the one-half percent was $18.9 million statewide, or only $2.1 million more than was spent on ESAs for students in the Davenport school district alone in the 2025-26 school year.


“You know who’s not complaining about a 1.75% increase?” Sen. Jesse Green, R-Harcourt, asked Feb. 10 during floor debate on the original version of SF 2201. “Those private schools. They’re working with a heck of a lot less, and they are happy.”
In 2022, the year before ESAs, Dowling Catholic High School’s tuition was $9,132 for parish families and $12,776 for non-parish families. In 2025, it was $11,076 plus $364 in fees for parish families and $15,498 plus fees for nonparish families. Dowling is also engaged in a $76 million capital campaign that did not require 60% supermajority approval from any public electorate.
Holy Family Catholic Schools in Dubuque raised its tuition from $2,200 in 2022 to $11,500 in 2025.
Siouxland Christian’s tuition went up 18% from 2024 to 2025.
Hull Christian School, which last year received more than $1.25 million in ESA money from students living in the Boyden-Hull school district, broke ground March 27 on a $4.7 million expansion.
Iowa does not require private schools to publish budgets or curriculum information. Iowa does not require them to have public meetings before major construction.
Private schools wouldn’t even have been bound by a bill of Wheeler’s that was approved by the House Education Committee on Feb. 11, but died later in the session, mandating that all students at public schools conform to a statewide dress code.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Conservative legal organization sues – again — over constitutionality of DFL’s 2024 omnibus
text:
House Minority Leader Lisa Demuth and Senate Minority Leader Mark Johnson spoke at a press conference shortly after the legislative session ended on May 20, 2024. The GOP leaders denounced the 1,400 page omnibus bill, which they displayed on the podium and was passed by the Democratic majority in the closing moments of the 2024 legislative session. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer.)A conservative legal organization is representing homebuilders in a lawsuit aimed at invalidating parts of — if not all of — a 1,400 page mega-bill passed by the DFL-controlled Legislature in the chaotic final minutes of the 2024 legislative session. 
The Minnesota Constitution requires that bills address a single subject, and that the title of the bill reflects that subject. Democratic-Farmer-Labor lawmakers assembled and passed the omnibus in the final shambolic hours of the 2024 legislative session following days of filibustering by Republican lawmakers, who shouted “Shame!” and “Follow the rules!” on the House floor as the DFL voted on the bill. 
The bill contained a wide range of new laws, from minimum pay rates for Uber and Lyft drivers to increased penalties for straw gun purchases and changes to the state’s paid leave law. The bill’s title was more than five pages long.
Previous plaintiffs suing over the same issue have already succeeded in getting parts of the bill overturned, and the continued litigation is a cautionary tale for future legislatures that try to cram all their bills into a mega-bill. Although the 2024 example is the most extreme in memory, legislative majorities of both parties have often loaded bills into mega-bills out of legislative and political expediency. 
Central Minnesota Builders Association and Rochester Area Builders Inc. are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed Monday by attorneys with the Upper Midwest Law Center. The lawsuit challenges the construction industry regulations in the bill, including restrictions on the use of independent contractors; new registration rules for construction companies; and, a requirement that the state residential energy code reduce net energy consumption by 70% by 2038.
The lawsuit asks that a state judge invalidate the entirety of the 2024 bill under the Constitution’s single subject clause — or to at least strike down its construction-related laws.
“This mega-omnibus bill creates an earthquake of increased costs and opportunities for fraud in our state,” said Nicholas Nelson, an attorney with the Upper Midwest Law Center. 
The Upper Midwest Law Center, representing the Minnesota Gun Owners Caucus, already successfully overturned one major policy provision in the bill: a ban on binary triggers, which increase the rate of fire of semiautomatic firearms. 
In that case, Ramsey County District Judge Leonardo Castro wrote that “the 2024 Omnibus Bill violates the Single Subject and Title Clause, because, at best, it contains many non-germane parts, and at worst, has no identifiable common theme.”
The ruling set the stage for further lawsuits from conservative organizations challenging other portions of the bill. Nelson said Monday’s lawsuit is the fifth such case.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s GOP Legislature left out key info on property taxes state question: the financial impact
text:
The downtown Oklahoma City skyline is pictured. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)If any emoji best represents the property tax state question Oklahoma lawmakers have placed before voters, it would be the grimace.
For those who need a translation, we use that face to express tension. In this case, it’s because our Republican-controlled Legislature, in all its wisdom, tacked on this disclaimer to their proposed constitutional amendment: “If passed, this measure would have a fiscal impact on the state, but the exact impact is unknown.”
(Insert eye-roll emoji.)
Lawmakers, in their zest to convince us they are cutting taxes as inflation rages on, decided that taking the time to suss out how eliminating a chunk of revenue via State Question 847 will affect senior citizens, public schools, CareerTechs, counties and some municipalities wasn’t as important as having a talking point on the campaign trail.
Because that’s where our property taxes go. Reminder: property taxes typically fund the functions of municipal and county governments. State government doesn’t get a dime from these taxes.  
Maybe that’s why they weren’t sure about the fiscal impact?
I don’t know whether this oversight was sheer laziness, a blatant disregard for voter intelligence or if legislators’ effort was a rush job that overlooked the finer details – including how complicated it probably is to calculate the impact.
But in any case, this is an unfair scenario for Oklahoma voters who have to make a decision on Nov. 3 about whether to change the structure of our property tax system. Voters deserve to have all the facts ahead of time, and lawmakers should not be permitted to omit them.
Since they did, though, I’ll fill in the gaps.
An Oklahoma Tax Commission analysis estimates local jurisdictions would lose about $45.78 million in revenue in the first year if voters approve this question. Over the next 10 years, that lost revenue could top $450 million.
That’s a whopping sum of money for a ballot measure that lists its fiscal impact as being “unknown.”
State Question 847 is one of the most convoluted and complicated state questions on the ballot this year, and that’s saying a lot given some of the other issues that lawmakers have placed before voters. (Who can forget that manufacturing tax credit that voters soundly rejected in August?)
Right now, the fair cash value of a home can’t increase by more than 3% a year for homesteads — better known as the homes we own and live in — and for most agricultural land. Commercial property values are capped at no more than a 5% annual increase.
Lawmakers have decided it’s time to lower that cap to a seemingly random 1.75% a year for homesteads and agricultural properties and to 4% for commercial properties. 
They also have decided to muck around with the income cap that senior citizens must meet to qualify for a valuation freeze. The amount of the increase would be calculated on a tiered system ranging from 0% to 1.75% based on a formula that is way too complicated.
Supporters argue that the measure would create the “lowest cap on growth” for homesteads in the U.S. and save cash-strapped Oklahomans money.
Critics, though, point out that besides the previously mentioned budget cuts for public schools, CareerTechs, county governments and some municipalities, it would also make it harder for those entities to borrow money for future needs.
They say this is not really property tax relief. The value of properties will continue to go up, and so will Oklahoman’s taxes. This merely just slows the rate of growth a bit.
But they also warn that because it will reduce revenue, many Oklahomans should expect to see their tax rates go up to pay the existing bills.
That’s because bond debt – that borrowed money I just mentioned – will not miraculously vanish. All bonds are set based on the revenue expected to be generated from existing property taxes. When someone screws around with the formula, it messes up those expected revenue streams.
The only feasible way right now to make up that lost revenue is to adjust the millage rates — better known as the tax rate assessed on real estate. That means everyone will see an increase in their taxes, but I suspect senior citizens living on fixed incomes could feel the pinch more.
Lower-income senior citizens’ home valuations have long been frozen to provide them an idea of what their tax bills will look like each year. Most probably have not budgeted to abruptly pay higher taxes.
How much millage rates will increase depends on how reliant an entity is on the revenue source and whether local jurisdictions have enough resources to adjust. 
Rural residents in particular will likely be harder hit because those entities have less resources to draw on. 
So instead of cutting expenses at the state government level that they control, lawmakers plan to force those cuts on local governments. How is that fair?
Oklahomans’ wallets definitely need relief from soaring property insurance and utility rates as well as high gas, diesel and grocery prices, but this plan doesn’t do anything to address that.
Maybe rather than monkeying around with our property tax formulas, lawmakers should first look at why their policies have resulted in us having the highest homeowners insurance rates in the country — more than double the national average. Reducing those rates would certainly provide welcome relief without harming our local revenue streams.
But it seems like state leaders prefer to live in a fairy tale where instead of apples or peaches, money grows on trees for the benefit of our cities and towns. And instead of doing the hard work of confronting insurance lobbyists and fixing broken state spending, it’s easier to ask voters to pass a plan with an unknown budgetary impact.
Here’s the reality: No business wants to come to a community that doesn’t have good schools, good roads and bridges and solid public services. Those services are primarily paid for by property taxes. 
To put this plan back in emoji speak: big red question mark.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT can opt to help students through a new federal tax program
text:
It seems everyone is talking about Nicole Hannah-Jones’ recent New York Times piece describing the educational experiences of her daughter, Najya, in the New York City public schools. If you haven’t read it, suffice to say that those experiences were less than ideal.
In recent days there have been dozens, if not hundreds, of commentaries on Hannah-Jones’ piece, and each one seems to have a different take on who is the villain in the story. Writing in the NY Post, Daniel di Martino insists that it is teacher’s unions. In the Free Press, Coleman Hughes suggests that an unwillingness to discipline disruptive children is a large part of the problem. In Slate, Jill Filipovic identifies no clear villain, but notes we need to make sure we are, ”not lowering the bar just because some students have a harder time clearing it.”
What all the commentators can agree on is that many, many schools in the United States are deeply dysfunctional. And, for this reason, many, many U.S. school children are receiving (as Hughes puts it in the Free Press), “[not just] a subpar education; they get no education, period.”
Fortunately, help is on the way. In 2025 the federal government created a provision that could put over $270 billion dollars every year into our educational system. The money would come from an optional tax credit (the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit) which, starting January 1, allows each U.S. citizen who owes at least $1,700 in taxes to (instead of paying tax) donate up to that amount to a scholarship granting organization (SGO) of his or her choice. Unlike a tax deduction, the credit means the donation is completely cost-free to the taxpayer.
The SGOs would take the money raised and use it to pay for educational expenses for children in their respective states.  The term SGO is a misnomer, since the money disbursed need not be a scholarship in a traditional sense.  It could be used for any “qualified elementary or secondary education expense” and could be given to both public and private school students.  The law specifically allows expenses as diverse as books, technology, tutoring, extended day programs and special needs services.
Hannah-Jones’ article points out that disadvantaged school districts typically have less money available to them even though their student bodies have higher needs.  This is primarily because public schools in the U.S. are mostly funded from local property tax receipts. Raising taxes is clearly not possible in poorer areas where citizens are already struggling to make ends meet. The new tax credit breaks down the correlation between local property tax revenues and resources available to schools, providing a new mechanism for monies to flow to under-resourced schools.
What is the catch, you ask? Only one. Any taxpayer is eligible to donate (again, at no cost to him or herself) to a qualified SGO. However, if you want your gift to go to help students in your state, your governor has to opt in to the program. If not, you can only donate to a scholarship granting organization in a state whose governor has opted in.
You would think it would be a no-brainer for states to opt-in. However, the IRS reports that as of October 13, 31 have done so and Connecticut is not one of them.  SGOs need time to plan to handle the new donations that will be coming in. 
Given the potential benefit to their neediest students, my only question is, “What is Connecticut waiting for?”
Christopher Rhoads is an associate professor in the Neag School of Education at the University of Connecticut.  The views expressed here are his own and do not represent those of his institution.
